title: Reading Between the Lines
theme: Literary analysis: irony, allusion and other devices
objectives: I can name literary devices such as irony, allusion, motif, archetype, and foil, and find an example of each in a story.
I can explain how foreshadowing and subtext give a story meaning that is not stated directly.
I can tell satire from parody, and tragic from merely sad.
I can use the prefixes fore- and sub- and the endings -ic and -ion to understand literary words.
rationale: Close reading of literature needs the names of the devices authors use and the verbs for how they work. Grade 8 students are asked not only to notice a repeated image or a hidden meaning but to say what it does, and these ten words give them the vocabulary. Six are Tier 3 literary terms (irony, allusion, satire, motif, archetype, foil) taught through one short invented story so that students can see them work together; the rest (foreshadow, subtext, parody, tragic) are Tier 2 words that critics use constantly. Allusion is a known confusable with illusion, and satire and parody are often swapped, so the unit sets each beside its look-alike. The unit builds on nuance, paradox, implicit, and ambiguous from the first unit, because every device here is a way of saying something without saying it outright.

words.def: A contrast between what is expected or said and what actually happens or is meant.
words.ex: It was an irony that the fire station burned down on the day of the fire-safety fair.
words.ex2: Her kind words had an edge of irony, since everyone knew she thought the plan was foolish.
words.nonExample: A rainy day during the rainy season is only expected weather, not irony.
words.rel: the opposite of what you expect

apps.academic: Irony in a story often exposes a gap between what a character believes and what the reader knows.
apps.spoken: There's a bit of irony in being late to a meeting about being on time.
apps.writing: Use irony for a gap between expectation and result, and name both sides of the gap.

cloze.s: The ___ of the story is that the safest-looking road is the one where the traveler gets lost.

cloze2.s: The speaker's ___ was clear when she said, "What a wonderful day," as rain poured through the roof.

misuse.s: It was irony when the weather forecast said rain and it rained exactly as predicted.
misuse.why: Irony needs a contrast between expectation and outcome; a correct prediction has none.

visual.alt: Two theater masks, one smiling and one frowning, turned in opposite directions.

words.def: A brief reference to a well-known person, event, story, or work that readers are expected to recognize.
words.ex: Calling a clear sky "the kind Noah would have wished for" is an allusion to the flood story.
words.ex2: The movie's title is an allusion to an old fairy tale, so viewers expect a story about a poisoned apple.
words.nonExample: An illusion is a trick that fools the eye; it is not an allusion.

apps.academic: To understand an allusion, readers must know the story or event the author is pointing to.
apps.spoken: That joke was an allusion to a famous movie; did you catch it?
apps.writing: Use allusion for a reference to another work or event; do not confuse it with illusion.

cloze.s: When the author called the city "a modern Eden," readers who knew the old garden story caught the ___.

cloze2.s: A passing ___ to a famous fable gave the editorial a deeper meaning for readers who knew the tale.

misuse.s: An allusion is a trick of light that makes a desert look like a lake.
misuse.why: That describes an illusion; an allusion is a reference to a known work or event.

visual.alt: A stack of books connected by a chain link.

words.def: A work that uses humor, exaggeration, or irony to criticize people's faults or society's problems.
words.ex: The newspaper's satire invented a town council that voted to cancel Mondays, poking fun at endless meetings.
words.ex2: Good satire makes readers laugh first and then notice the real problem behind the joke.
words.nonExample: A joke that is only silly, with no point about people's behavior, is not satire.

apps.academic: A satirist exaggerates a real habit, such as vanity, so that readers see it clearly.
apps.spoken: That show is satire; it makes fun of how people behave online.
apps.writing: Use satire for humor with a critical point, and name what is being criticized.

cloze.s: The comic strip was a sharp ___ of people who spend more time posing for photos than enjoying a trip.

cloze2.s: Readers laughed at the ___, but the writer's real aim was to criticize the careless way the town spent its money.

misuse.s: The writer's satire was a gentle poem that praised everyone and criticized no one.
misuse.why: Satire criticizes through humor; a poem that praises everyone does not.

visual.alt: A clown holding up a newspaper.

words.frame: The satire makes fun of ___ to show that ___.

words.def: A repeated image, idea, sound, or pattern in a work that helps build its meaning.
words.ex: Water is a motif in the novel: rain, rivers, and puddles appear in almost every chapter.
words.ex2: A recurring bell in the film is a motif that rings each time a character makes a choice.
words.nonExample: An image that appears once and is never mentioned again is not a motif.

apps.academic: To track a motif, list each place it appears and ask what changes each time.
apps.spoken: There's a motif of doors in this story; I keep seeing them.
apps.writing: Use motif for a repeated element, and explain what the repetition adds to the meaning.

cloze.s: The broken clock is a ___ in the story, appearing in each scene where someone wishes for more time.

cloze2.s: A recurring song gives the play a musical ___ that ties its scenes together.

misuse.s: A motif is an image that appears exactly one time and is never mentioned again.
misuse.why: A motif is repeated, not one-time.

visual.alt: A repeat arrow beside a musical note.

words.frame: The motif of ___ appears when ___ and suggests ___.

words.def: A very typical example or pattern of a character, setting, or situation that appears again and again in stories.
words.ex: The wise old mentor who guides a young hero is an archetype found in many stories.
words.ex2: The trickster is an archetype: a clever character who breaks the rules and causes trouble.
words.nonExample: A character with strange habits that are unlike any other in literature is unique, not an archetype.

apps.academic: Readers recognize an archetype quickly, and good authors may follow it or surprise us by breaking it.
apps.spoken: The brave hero who leaves home is a classic archetype.
apps.writing: Use archetype for a familiar pattern of character or plot, and note how the author follows or changes it.

cloze.s: The brave youngest sibling who sets out to save the family is a familiar ___ in fairy tales.

cloze2.s: Because the villain was a perfect ___ of greed, readers could predict how the story would end.

misuse.s: An archetype is a one-of-a-kind character who has never appeared in any story before.
misuse.why: An archetype is a familiar pattern that appears repeatedly, not a one-of-a-kind creation.

visual.alt: A wizard figure standing on an open storybook.

words.frame: The character is an archetype of ___ because ___.

words.def: A character whose qualities contrast with another character's, making the other's qualities stand out.

senses.def: To prevent someone from succeeding in a plan.
senses.example: The guard foiled the thief's plan by locking the back door.

words.ex: Quiet, careful Maria is a foil for her impulsive brother, because her patience makes his rushing more obvious.
words.ex2: In the play, the cheerful servant is a foil to the gloomy king.
words.nonExample: A character who is exactly like the hero does not serve as a foil.

apps.academic: An author may use a foil to highlight a protagonist's flaw without ever stating it.
apps.spoken: Her calm voice is a foil for his loud one.
apps.writing: Use foil for a character who contrasts with another, and name the trait that is made clearer.

cloze.s: The calm neighbor serves as a ___ to the boastful forecaster, making his pride more obvious.

cloze2.s: A good ___ is not simply the villain; it is any character whose differences help us see the hero more clearly.

misuse.s: The foil was the main hero's twin, identical in every trait, with nothing to contrast.
misuse.why: A foil contrasts with another character; an identical twin does not.

visual.alt: A black circle beside a white circle.

words.def: To give a hint early in a story about something that will happen later.
words.ex: The dark clouds in the first paragraph foreshadow the storm that traps the characters in the final scene.
words.ex2: A character's unusual fear of stairs foreshadows the fall that happens later in the book.
words.nonExample: Telling the ending in the first sentence reveals it; it does not foreshadow it.

apps.academic: Foreshadowing makes a surprising ending feel earned, because the clues were there all along.
apps.spoken: That strange noise in the first chapter really foreshadowed the ending.
apps.writing: Use foreshadow for a hint planted earlier, and say what later event it prepares.

cloze.s: The cracked mirror in chapter one seems to ___ the broken friendship that comes at the end.

cloze2.s: Authors often ___ a surprise by planting a small clue that readers notice only on a second reading.

misuse.s: The author foreshadowed the ending by explaining what happened ten years earlier.
misuse.why: To foreshadow is to hint at a future event, not to explain the past.

visual.alt: Dark clouds above a crystal ball.

words.def: The unspoken meaning beneath what characters actually say or do.
words.ex: The words of the apology were polite, but the subtext was that he did not think he had done anything wrong.
words.ex2: Actors work hard to show subtext, because a look can say more than a line.
words.nonExample: A character who announces, "I am angry!" leaves nothing to subtext.

apps.academic: To find subtext, compare what a character says with what the character does and what the scene suggests.
apps.spoken: The subtext of her answer was that she wasn't coming.
apps.writing: Use subtext for the unspoken meaning, and point to the words or actions that suggest it.

cloze.s: When she said, "Nice of you to remember," the ___ was that he had forgotten her birthday twice.

cloze2.s: The scene has little spoken drama, yet its ___ about loneliness is powerful.

misuse.s: Subtext is the part of a story that is printed in large letters on the first page.
misuse.why: Subtext is meaning beneath the words, not visible text.

visual.alt: An ice cube floating beside a speech bubble.

words.def: A humorous imitation of a work, style, or person that exaggerates its features to make fun of it.
words.ex: The class wrote a parody of a superhero movie in which the hero is afraid of paperwork.
words.ex2: A parody of a cooking show can exaggerate every habit of the host until viewers laugh.
words.nonExample: A serious copy that tries to match the original exactly, with no joke, is not a parody.

apps.academic: A parody works only if readers recognize the original, because the humor comes from the exaggeration.
apps.spoken: That video is a parody of a famous commercial.
apps.writing: Use parody for a funny imitation of a specific work or style, and name what is being imitated.

cloze.s: The comedy troupe's ___ of a news broadcast exaggerated every pause, frown, and dramatic headline.

cloze2.s: To write a ___, you must know the original well enough to copy its style and then twist it for laughs.

misuse.s: A parody is a serious and respectful copy of a work that tries to avoid any humor.
misuse.why: A parody is a humorous imitation, not a serious copy.

visual.alt: A film clapperboard beside a silly face.

words.frame: The parody exaggerates ___ to make fun of ___.

words.def: Involving great suffering or loss, especially when it comes from a character's flaw or from fate.
words.ex: The play ends with a tragic misunderstanding that costs the young couple everything.
words.ex2: A tragic hero, such as a proud king, brings about his own downfall through a flaw in his character.
words.nonExample: Losing a pencil is annoying, but it is not tragic.

apps.academic: In a tragic plot, the hero's choices and flaws lead step by step toward the downfall.
apps.spoken: It was a tragic ending, and the whole class was quiet.
apps.writing: Use tragic for serious loss or downfall; avoid it for minor disappointments.

cloze.s: The story is ___ because the hero's pride leads him to lose everything he loves.

cloze2.s: In the ___ final scene, the family realizes too late that they should have listened to one another.

misuse.s: The story had a tragic ending because everyone celebrated and nothing bad ever happened.
misuse.why: Tragic means involving great loss; a happy ending is not tragic.

visual.alt: A theater mask beside a broken heart.

passage.title: The Umbrella Man
paras: Ms. Park read her class a short story called "The Umbrella Man." In it, a weather forecaster named Gus carries an umbrella everywhere and laughs at people who worry about rain. On the day of the town parade, the sky is perfectly clear, and Gus forgets his umbrella for the first time. A storm arrives out of nowhere and soaks him in front of the whole town.

"Notice the irony," Ms. Park said. "A forecaster cannot predict his own day." Lena had spotted an earlier line: "Gus checked the sky twice and promised that nobody would get wet." "That foreshadows the storm," Lena said. "It hints at what is coming." Dev pointed out that the story kept returning to rain, clouds, and puddles. "That is a motif," said Ms. Park, "a repeated image that builds meaning."

She asked about the neighbor, who says, "Lovely day, isn't it?" with a stiff smile as Gus passes. "The words are polite," Dev said, "but the subtext is that she knows he is wrong." Priya added that the narrator calls the clear sky "the kind Noah would have wished for." "That is an allusion," said Ms. Park, "to the flood story that many readers know."

Tomas asked whether the neighbor was a foil. "Yes," said Ms. Park. "Her calm makes his boasting easier to see." Priya thought Gus was an archetype, the proud man who is humbled. "And is the story tragic?" Ms. Park asked. "Not at all," Tomas said. "The only loss is a wet shirt." The class laughed.

Ms. Park explained that the story was also a gentle satire, because it used humor to criticize overconfidence. For homework, she asked the class to write a parody of it, imitating its style to make fun of the story itself.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, Ms. Park says the story contains "irony." In this context, irony means
choices: a gap between what is expected and what happens
a character who tells the truth
a lesson that the story teaches
a description of a storm
qs.why: The forecaster who cannot predict his own day shows a contrast between what we expect of him and what happens.

qs.q: According to Dev, what is the subtext of the neighbor's remark, "Lovely day, isn't it?"
choices: She is sincerely admiring the weather.
She is quietly signaling that she knows Gus is wrong about the storm.
She wants to leave the parade.
She is angry at the narrator.
qs.why: Dev says the words are polite, but the subtext is that she knows he is wrong, and the stiff smile hints at what she does not say.

qs.q: Which line from the story best shows foreshadowing?
choices: "Lovely day, isn't it?"
"Gus checked the sky twice and promised that nobody would get wet."
"The kind Noah would have wished for."
"The only loss is a wet shirt."
qs.why: Lena notes that Gus's promise hints at the storm that follows and shows what will happen.

qs.q: Why does Tomas say the story is not tragic?
choices: It was written by an unknown author.
It takes place in a small town.
It has no weather in it.
The only loss is small and funny, not a serious downfall.
qs.why: Tomas says the only loss is a wet shirt, and tragic would require serious suffering or downfall.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
choices: A short story cannot have more than one device.
Authors use devices such as irony, motifs, and foils to create meaning that readers can find by close reading.
Stories about weather are always funny.
Readers should avoid thinking about subtext.
qs.why: Ms. Park and her students find irony, foreshadowing, a motif, subtext, allusion, a foil, and an archetype and explain how each shapes the story.

write.prompt: Choose a story, film, or song you know well. Name one device from this unit that it uses (such as irony, a motif, or foreshadowing) and explain how it adds meaning, using at least three words from the unit.
write.frame: In ___, the author uses ___ when ___. This adds meaning because ___.

parts.m: relating to; having the nature of

study.task: Choose foreshadow and subtext. Break each into its two parts and say what each part means. Then explain how the parts help you remember what the word means in a story, and write a sentence that uses both words about the same story.

groups.label: patterns and references that build meaning
meaning that works under the surface
kinds of writing and their effects

author : poem

sentences: Write a sentence about a moment of irony you have seen in a story, film, or real life. Name both sides of the contrast.
Write a sentence that uses both foreshadow and subtext to describe a scene in which a small clue hints at a hidden feeling.

given: The story repeats an image of a locked door.
The door appears in every chapter.
combine.model: The locked door is a motif in the story, appearing in every chapter and standing for secrets.

given: The comedy copied the style of a spy film.
combine.model: The comedy was a parody of a spy film, exaggerating every dramatic pause to make the audience laugh.

discuss: Can a story be both tragic and ironic? Explain with tragic and irony.
What is the difference between a parody and a satire? Use both words and give an example of each.
Why might an author use an allusion instead of explaining the reference directly?
produce.explain: Explain how subtext can show a character's feelings without the character saying them. Use subtext and one other word from the unit.

argue.prompt: Claim: Authors should use foreshadowing so that surprises feel fair to readers. Take a side and support it with two reasons using words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. A story with foreshadowing could ___, but a story without it might ___.

constructed.prompt: A story has a proud knight and a humble farmer who helps him. Use foil and archetype to describe each character's role.
look: identifies the knight as an archetype and the farmer as a contrast
explains how the contrast reveals a trait
constructed.model: The proud knight is an archetype of the boastful hero, and the humble farmer is a foil whose modesty makes the knight's pride clearer.

constructed.prompt: A character spends the whole story preparing for a flood. In the last scene, a fire destroys her house instead. Use irony, foreshadow, and tragic to analyze what the author does.
look: explains a hint that foreshadows the fire or the seriousness of the loss
constructed.model: The irony is that she prepares for the wrong danger. Earlier details, such as a flickering lamp, could foreshadow the fire. The loss of her home makes the ending tragic.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for analyzing literature, read a short narrative about a class discussing a story, practice the prefixes fore- and sub- and the endings -ic and -ion, and write about a device in a text they know. The key habit is to name the device and then explain what it adds.

notes.va.irony.n: Irony is a gap between expectation and result. Students often use ironic for coincidence or bad luck; require them to name both sides of the contrast. Avoid teaching all three types (verbal, situational, dramatic) at once; start with the one in the passage.
notes.va.allusion.n: Allusion is a reference to something readers know. It is a confusable with illusion, so write both and have students use each in a sentence. Draw on stories students know (fairy tales, folktales) and avoid examples that depend on religious background unless they are part of the curriculum.
notes.va.satire.n: Satire criticizes through humor. Parody imitates to make fun. Use a Venn diagram. Ask 'what is being criticized?' for satire and 'what is being imitated?' for parody. Choose school-appropriate examples.
notes.va.motif.n: A motif is a repeated element that builds meaning. Students sometimes confuse it with theme. A motif is a repeated image or pattern; the theme is the message the repetition helps to build. Have students track one motif across scenes.
notes.va.archetype.n: An archetype is a familiar pattern of character or plot. Students may think it is the same as a stereotype; stress that an archetype is a pattern that authors can follow or change, while a stereotype is an unfair simplification of a group.
notes.va.foil.n: Foil is a character who contrasts. The second sense (to prevent) is shown on the word card. Draw a two-column chart of traits for the hero and the foil. Ask what the author wants us to notice by placing the two together.
notes.va.foreshadow.v: Foreshadow is fore- (before) + shadow. Students find it easier to spot foreshadowing on a second reading; reread a short story and underline the clues. Distinguish foreshadow from predict: authors foreshadow, readers predict.
notes.va.subtext.n: Subtext is the unspoken meaning. Link to implicit from unit 1. Practice by acting out a line two ways. Model sub- (under) + text. English learners may need practice reading tone and gesture.
notes.va.parody.n: Parody is a funny imitation that depends on knowing the original. It is not the same as satire, though they can overlap. Use a short example, such as an imitation of a news broadcast. Keep parodies kind and avoid targeting real students or staff.
notes.va.tragic.adj: Tragic is stronger than sad. In literature it often involves a serious downfall linked to a flaw or to fate. Students overuse the word for small misfortunes; use the pencil example to separate tragic from annoying.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The forecaster is sure of himself and the storm still gets him, so there is irony. Earlier, the line that nobody would get wet hints at the storm, so that is foreshadowing. The neighbor's polite words and stiff smile have subtext. Her calm makes his boasting stand out, so she is a foil. I can name each device and say what it adds.'

How can a parody also work as satire?
misconceptions: Irony just means something unlucky or coincidental.
Allusion and illusion are the same word.
Satire and parody always mean the same thing.
A tragic story is any story that is sad.
extend: Choose a short story and make a chart of one motif across three scenes, with a note on what it adds each time.
Write a short parody of a story or ad the class knows, and then explain what you exaggerated and why.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit irony, foreshadow, and subtext within two days by finding one in a new short text, and at one week by writing a short paragraph that names and explains a device. The unit 1 words nuance, paradox, implicit, and ambiguous return as ways to describe how a device creates meaning without saying it outright.

wida.oral: Partner A reads a short passage aloud. Partner B names one device from the unit (irony, motif, foreshadowing, or subtext), points to the words that show it, and says what it adds to the passage.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: ironía, alusión, sátira, motivo, arquetipo, personaje contrastante (foil; no single standard term), presagiar (foreshadow; anticipar is another choice), subtexto, parodia, trágico.
Cognate flags for ironía, alusión, sátira, motivo, arquetipo, subtexto, parodia, and trágico should be confirmed.

Facts: the allusion to the flood story and Noah in the passage and in one example is a general reference to a widely known story; no claim about a specific text is made. The Umbrella Man and all characters are fictional.
Sense boundaries: foil has a verb sense (to prevent), shown as a second sense. Morphology: foreshadow is shown as fore- plus shadow; subtext and tragic have no morph breakdown beyond the study parts.
